text: Chapter two gave you maturity models — where an organization sits on a governance continuum. Now it's time to actually find out where yours sits, before you design anything.

Skipping the assessment is the number-one reason governance programs stall. A team buys a catalog tool, writes a charter, forms a council — and six months later nothing's changed, because nobody checked for sponsorship, capacity, or whether the business even agreed there was a problem. Technology was never the gap. Readiness was.

A real readiness check rates six independent dimensions: current data practices, executive sponsorship, organizational structure, existing policy, technology and tooling, and regulatory pressure. Rate each one Low, Medium, or High on its own — an organization can be strong on one and weak on another, and that combination tells you something.

An assessment run entirely by IT produces a technology inventory, not a readiness assessment. You need the prospective executive sponsor, a few business data owners who can name real pain points, IT and data engineering, compliance or legal, and a handful of frontline data consumers. Fifteen minutes with each beats a survey nobody fills out.

The assessment only matters if it produces a gap list — current rating, target rating, and the one-line gap, per dimension. That list feeds directly into next lesson's business case and the lesson after that's pilot selection. The gaps are the justification.

Three traps to avoid: mistaking tooling for readiness, skipping business engagement so IT rates itself too generously, and treating the assessment as a one-time event instead of something you redo after a leadership change or a new regulation.
Six dimensions, the right people in the room, and a gap list at the end — that's a real readiness assessment. Next up: turning that gap list into a business case someone will actually fund.
